standard_prerequisites.name: Well-order
standard_prerequisites.statement: A relation < well-orders A when it is a strict linear order on A in which every non-empty subset of A has a <-least element.
standard_prerequisites.use: The statement assumes < well-orders A and the proof uses the existence of a <-minimal element of the non-empty set X of counterexamples (source line 1276).

standard_prerequisites.name: Transfinite induction schema over a well-order
standard_prerequisites.statement: The schema asserted here: if for every a in A, (for all b < a) phi(b) implies phi(a), then phi(a) holds for every a in A, for an arbitrary formula phi with parameters.
standard_prerequisites.use: This is the counted proposition itself; the proof establishes it by contraposition rather than by a direct induction, so no further induction principle is assumed.

standard_prerequisites.name: Set abstraction and non-empty subset
standard_prerequisites.statement: X = {x in A : not phi(x)} is the subset of A collecting the counterexamples to phi, and phi may carry parameters.
standard_prerequisites.use: The proof forms this set at source lines 1275-1276 and applies well-ordering to it once it is known to be non-empty.

core_obligations: Reformulate the assertion as a contrapositive: assume not (for all a in A) phi(a) and derive the failure of the premise (source lines 1274-1275).
Form the set X = {x in A : not phi(x)} and observe that the assumed failure makes X non-empty (source lines 1275-1276).

Apply the well-ordering of A to X to obtain a <-minimal element a of X, so that every b < a satisfies phi(b) while phi(a) fails (source lines 1276-1277), which denies the premise (for all a in A)((for all b < a) phi(b) implies phi(a)) and completes the contrapositive.

proof_roadmap.step: Switch to the contrapositive: suppose not every element of A satisfies phi, and introduce phi's counterexamples.
Collect the counterexamples into the set X = {x in A : not phi(x)}; the supposition makes X non-empty.
Take a <-minimal element a of X; then all b < a satisfy phi while a does not, so the induction premise fails, giving the contrapositive.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the author's own proposition propwoinduction at source lines 1265-1271: for a well-order < on A and an arbitrary formula phi(x), (for all a in A)((for all b < a) phi(b) implies phi(a)) implies (for all a in A) phi(a). The proof at source lines 1273-1277 is short but is not a routine instance of an induction rule stated earlier: it must recognise that the schema is equivalent to its contrapositive, that the counterexample set X = {x in A : not phi(x)} must be formed so that well-ordering can be applied to it, and that the <-minimal element of X yields simultaneously (for all b < a) phi(b) and not phi(a). The statement is quantified over an arbitrary formula with parameters, so the argument has to be read as a schema rather than as a single proposition. No standard result outside the retained text is used: the whole argument stays inside the well-ordering definition and set abstraction.

compared.difference: That candidate (statement 1250-1253, proof 1255-1263) counts the elementary consequences of the definition of a well-order — unique least element, irreflexivity, asymmetry, transitivity — and its proof reasons about finite subsets {a}, {a,b,c}. Our candidate counts the induction schema and reasons about the counterexample set X and its minimal element; neither statement implies the other as a card.

ordinductionschema is the schema of transfinite induction stated for ordinals themselves (a class-theoretic formulation proved from the definition of an ordinal), whereas propwoinduction is stated for any well-order and is proved directly by contraposition from the least-element property. Different domains, different proofs.
